item.title: Cherry Hallway Console (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — fully dimensioned and detailed, but not yet cut. A narrow wall console for an entry/hallway: drop keys and mail on top, baskets or shoes on the lower shelf. Solid cherry, hand-tool build (stock ripped and thickness-planed by machine; all joinery cut by hand).

  • Overall size: 42" W × 14" D × 34" H
  • Top overhang: 1" all around the leg frame
  • Lower shelf: ~10" off the floor, resting on the lower rails
  • Joinery: mortise-and-tenon frame, drawbored; floating solid top

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 12 px from the dimensions on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

Variant: want somewhere to sit and put shoes on? See Cherry Console + Slide-Under Chest Bench — the same console with an open lower half and a blanket-chest seat that slides underneath.

Why these proportions

The shallow 14" depth is the point of a hallway piece — it hugs the wall and stays out of the traffic path. 34" tall sits at about waist height, comfortable for setting things down (anywhere 30–34" works; taller reads more console-like). 42" long gives presence without dominating a corridor. Legs are 1½" square — slender but honest for this span; go to 1¾" if you want it chunkier. The lower shelf earns its keep both as storage and as a structural tie that stiffens the whole frame.

Materials

Species: solid cherry, clear finish. Cherry darkens dramatically with light over the first few months (pale pink → deep reddish-brown) — plan around that (see notes).

Stock Used for Rough qty (approx)
8/4 (2" rough) Legs only 5–6 bd ft
4/4 (1" rough) Top, aprons, lower rails, shelf 18–20 bd ft

Only the legs need stock heavier than 4/4. A finished 1½"-square leg cannot come out of 4/4 — rough 4/4 only nets ~¾" of flat, clean stock after jointing and planing out cup/twist. Buy 8/4 and keep the legs seamless. (6/4 is too close to 1½" finished to survive jointing unless you drop the legs to ~1⅜".)

Lamination alternative: two face-glued pieces of 4/4 make a ~1½" blank, but on a 1½"-square leg the glue line lands on two visible faces and will age to a slightly different shade. On a clear-finished cherry piece, 8/4 is worth it. If you do laminate, orient the seam to a back corner.

The 4/4 estimate leaves margin for grain-matching the top and shelf glue-ups and for working around cherry’s gum streaks and sapwood.

Cut list

Dimensions are thickness × width × length. Cut to the length in the table — the tenon lengths are already baked in.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L (cut to this) Tenons / notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½" × 1½" × 33¼" Mortised on two adjacent faces
Long aprons (front/back) 2 4/4 ¾" × 3½" × 39" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Short aprons (sides) 2 4/4 ¾" × 3½" × 11" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Long lower rails (front/back) 2 4/4 ¾" × 2½" × 39" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Short lower rails (sides) 2 4/4 ¾" × 2½" × 11" 1" tenon each end, mitered tips
Top 1 4/4 ¾" × 14" × 42" No joinery; floats on frame
Lower shelf 1 4/4 ¾" × 12" × 40" Notch corners 1½" × 1½"; rests on rails

Key reference dimensions

  • Shoulder-to-shoulder (what actually keeps the frame square):
    • Long aprons & long rails: 37"
    • Short aprons & short rails: 9"
  • The extra 2" on each part = two 1" tenons living inside the legs. Set your shoulder gauge to 37" / 9" and the tenon length falls out on its own.
  • Mortises: ~5/16" wide × ~1" deep. Two tenons meet inside each leg corner — miter their tips at 45° so they don’t collide.

Build sequence

  1. Mill 4/4 down to a true ¾" in stages, resting between passes — cherry moves as internal tension releases. Leave leg blanks a hair oversized off the planer and take the last shaving by hand.
  2. Lay out and cut all mortises and tenons. Fit each tenon to its mortise before any glue-up.
  3. Glue up two end units: each = a pair of legs + short apron + short lower rail.
  4. Connect the two ends with the long aprons and long rails.
  5. Dry-clamp the whole frame and confirm the 37" and 9" shoulder distances land square before committing.
  6. Drawbore the tenons — pins pull the joints tight without clamping across the 42" span. See Drawboring below for sizes and the step-by-step.
  7. Drop the shelf onto the four lower rails.
  8. Attach the top with figure-8 fasteners or wooden buttons so the solid top can float (expand/contract seasonally). Do not glue the top down.

Drawboring

Drawboring means the pin hole in the leg and the pin hole in the tenon are deliberately about 1/32″ out of line. A tapered pin driven through both pulls the tenon deeper into the mortise and closes the shoulder, then locks the joint mechanically. On a 42″ frame that replaces a long clamp, and the joint stays tight even if the glue ever lets go.

The blue hole is drilled in the leg; the red hole is drilled in the tenon, centered 1/32″ nearer the shoulder. The drawing is true to scale.

Sizes for this table

Item Value Why
Pin diameter 1/8″ The tenon is only 5/16″ thick; a 1/4″ pin would leave ~1/32″ of wood each side
Offset 1/32″ toward the shoulder Hardwood pins this small tolerate up to ~3/64″; more can crush or split the tenon
Pin position ½″ in from the leg face Mid-tenon on a 1″ tenon, clear of the end grain and of the mitered tip of the neighboring tenon
Pins per tenon 2 on the 3½″ aprons (about 1″ from each edge); 1–2 on the 2½″ rails Spreads the pull across the width of the tenon
Hole depth in leg Through the near wall, across the mortise, ¼″ into the far wall Blind, so no pin end shows on the far side

Stagger the pins at each leg corner. Two tenons meet inside the leg, and their pins are drilled from the two adjacent outer faces. If the long-apron pin and the short-apron pin sit at the same height they cross inside the leg. Put the long-apron pins at about ¾″ and 2¾″ below the top edge, and the short-apron pin at about 1¾″ (mid-height).

Steps

  1. Cut and fit every mortise and tenon dry. It should seat by hand or with light taps, not with force.
  2. Drill the leg. Use a sharp brad-point bit and a backing block. Start on the leg’s outer face (so the pin dots show on the faces that are meant to be seen) and drill square through the near wall, across the mortise, and ¼″ into the far wall.
  3. Mark the tenon. Seat the tenon fully, put the bit back into the leg hole and tap it so the point dimples the tenon cheek.
  4. Offset and drill the tenon. Pull the tenon, move the mark 1/32″ toward the shoulder, and drill at that new mark. A drill press with a fence keeps it square to the cheek; clamp scrap behind to prevent blowout.
  5. Make the pins. Straight-grain cherry or 1/8″ hardwood dowel, with a 3/8″ taper at the tip so it finds the offset hole.
  6. Glue-up. Glue on the tenon cheeks and shoulders, none on the pins. Seat the joint, then drive the pin until it stops; you should feel the shoulder draw in.
  7. When the glue has set, saw the pins flush and scrape them clean.

For this build

  • Do the end units first (short, easy), then assemble the long aprons and rails into both ends together. Use hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you are not racing the clock over 42″.
  • Drive the pins one corner at a time. A single pipe clamp is only for starting the joints, not for holding them.
  • Test on scrap first: make one joint in cherry with the same 5/16″ tenon and 1/8″ pin. A good result is a closed shoulder with no cracks around the pin; if the tenon splits, reduce the offset.

Domino option

A Festool Domino can cut the apron joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The plan’s 5/16″ mortise is 7.9 mm, so an 8 mm Domino matches it, and a 40 mm Domino sits 20 mm (¾″) deep in each part.

The one rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside a 1½″ leg. The hand-cut plan avoids that by mitering the tenon tips. Loose tenons can’t be mitered, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them.

Joint Domino Cut length (was)
Long aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 24 mm (≈ ⅞″) below the apron’s top edge 37″ (39″)
Short aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 66 mm (≈ 2⅝″) below the apron’s top edge 9″ (11″)
Lower rails (×4) Keep the hand-cut mitered tenons 39″ and 11″ (unchanged)
  • With the Domino, cut length = shoulder-to-shoulder (37″ and 9″); there is no tenon allowance to add.
  • Keep the aprons flush to the leg faces and centre each 8 mm mortise on the apron’s ¾″ thickness.
  • The 2½″ lower rails are too short to stagger two 40 mm Dominoes at the same corner, so they stay hand-cut. Their mortises sit well below the apron Dominoes, so nothing collides.
  • One 8×40 Domino has noticeably less glue area than the full-width tenon it replaces. That is fine for a hallway console; the lower rails and shelf stiffen the frame.
  • Drawboring does not carry over to the Domino joints (a 1/8″ pin through an 8 mm Domino is marginal). Clamp the aprons instead, with hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you can square a 42″ frame before it sets.

Hand-tool & cherry notes

  • Tear-out: cherry planes beautifully but tears where grain reverses (near figure or the pith). Keep the smoother sharp and finely set, read grain direction before each pass, and keep a card scraper handy for the top glue-up and any tricky patches.
  • Color / clamps: don’t leave clamps, tape, or stickers on exposed surfaces during glue-up or curing — cherry tans unevenly and you’ll get pale patches that never catch up.
  • Squeeze-out: scrape off all glue squeeze-out before finishing. Finish over dried glue blocks the darkening and leaves permanent ghost lines.

Adjustments to consider

  • Stretch to 48" long, or drop height to 30".
  • Add a drawer in the front apron (would change the front apron to a rail + drawer pocket).
  • Bump legs to 1¾" square for a heavier look (still cut from 8/4).

item.title: Cherry Console + Slide-Under Chest Bench (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed two-piece build: the Cherry Hallway Console reworked so its lower half is open, plus a separate blanket chest that doubles as a seat and slides underneath. Sit on the lid to put shoes on; push the chest in and the hallway looks like a plain console. Solid cherry, drawbored mortise-and-tenon frame, dovetailed chest.

Everything here is my own design, so there are no maker dimensions to match. Every number is a design choice or derived from one, and the fit checks below show how the two pieces close.

What changes from the original console

Original This version Why
Overall 42″ × 14″ × 34″ 42″ × 15″ × 35″ 1″ deeper so the seat is 13″ deep (shoe-tying depth); 1″ taller so the lid can open fully under the apron
Lower shelf Yes, ≈ 10″ off floor Removed The chest lives there
Front lower rail Yes Removed The chest slides in through the front
Back lower rail Yes Kept — now the chest’s stop
Side lower rails Yes Kept The chest passes between them
Leg frame 40″ × 12″ 40″ × 13″

How the two pieces fit

Check Working Result
Opening between front legs 40 − 2 × 1½ 37″
Chest width 37 − 2 × ½ clearance 36″
Side rails, inner faces 40 − 2 × ¾ 38½″ apart — chest never touches them
Clear height under the apron 35 − ¾ top − 3½ apron 30¾″
Seat (lid top) height design choice 17″ — a normal bench height
Space above the lid 30¾ − 17 13¾″
Lid depth (hinged at the back) 13″
Lid front edge, open to vertical 17 + 13 30″, so ¾″ below the apron
Back stop 15 − 1 − ¾ (back rail) chest back at 13¼″ from the front edge
Chest front 13¼ − 13 ¼″ behind the top’s front edge, ¾″ proud of the legs

The lid opens all the way with the chest pushed fully under — the lid’s front edge swings up an arc of radius 13″ and clears the apron by ¾″. A deeper chest or a taller seat would break that, so the 17″ × 13″ pair is the limit for this console. For comfortable access to blankets, slide the chest out a few inches first.

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 12 px (the chest section at 1″ = 16 px). Click to open full size.

Front elevation, chest pushed in

Side elevation, lid open to vertical

Plan view, top removed

Chest end section

Console

Joinery and finishing are the same as the original plan: mortise-and-tenon, 1″ tenons, drawbored, floating top on buttons or figure-8s. See its Drawboring section for pin sizes and steps.

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length. Tenon lengths are baked in.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½″ × 1½″ × 34¼″
Long aprons (front, back) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 3½″ × 39″ 37″ shoulder to shoulder
Short aprons (sides) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 3½″ × 12″ 10″ shoulder to shoulder
Side lower rails 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2½″ × 12″ Top edge ≈ 9¼″ off the floor, flush to the leg outer face
Back lower rail 1 4/4 ¾″ × 2½″ × 39″ The chest’s stop; glue a ¼″ felt strip on its inner face
Top 1 4/4 ¾″ × 15″ × 42″ Floats; 1″ overhang all round

Stiffness without a front lower rail

With the front rail gone, the base is braced on three sides (two side rails and the back rail) and the top is a rigid box of four 3½″ aprons. That is enough for a hallway piece, but it relies on the joints: drawbore the apron joints, and dry-assemble to check there is no racking along the 42″ length before you glue. If the front legs still flex, add a hidden gusset block at each front leg-to-apron corner.

Chest bench

Cut list

Cherry for everything visible. T × W × L.

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Lid 1 5/4 1″ × 13″ × 36″ Glue up from two boards; cleat underneath (below)
Case front, back 2 4/4 ¾″ × 13¾″ × 36″ Through dovetails; ¼″ groove for the bottom
Case ends 2 4/4 ¾″ × 13¾″ × 13″ Through dovetails; ¼″ groove for the bottom
Bottom 1 ½″ ½″ × 11⅞″ × 35″ Cherry or ply; floats in the grooves, grain along the length if solid
Plinth front, back 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2¼″ × 35¼″ Mitered corners, inset ⅜″ all round
Plinth ends 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2¼″ × 12¼″ Mitered corners
Lid cleats 2 4/4 ¾″ × 1¼″ × 11¼″ Underside, 2″ in from each end; slotted screw holes so the lid can move

Height is 1″ lid + 13¾″ case + 2¼″ plinth = 17″. The interior is about 34½″ × 11½″ × 13¼″.

Hardware

  • Hinge: one 36″ continuous (piano) hinge, 1½″ open, mortised into the back edge of the lid and case.
  • Lid support: two soft-close lid stays rated for the lid’s weight (≈ 10 lb), so it can’t slam on fingers.
  • Glides: four PTFE or felt glide pads under the plinth so the chest slides on a hard floor.
  • Edges: ease the lid edges ⅛″–¼″; they are where you sit.

Build sequence

  1. Mill case, lid and plinth stock and let it settle between passes.
  2. Cut and fit the through dovetails on the case. Plow the ¼″ bottom grooves before assembly.
  3. Glue up the case with the bottom dry (unglued) in its grooves.
  4. Make the plinth, miter the corners, and glue it to the case bottom edge — long grain to long grain, so glue is fine.
  5. Glue up the lid, add the cleats, and mortise the hinge into lid and case.
  6. Hang the lid and fit the stays. Check the lid opens to vertical with the chest in place under the console.
  7. Finish with hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax; add glides last.

Open questions

  • Seat depth. 13″ is comfortable for shoes but shallow for general sitting. Going deeper means a deeper, taller console so the lid still clears; the arc check above is the thing to redo.
  • Console leg section. 1½″ legs were fine for the original shelf version; with the front rail gone you may prefer 1¾″.
  • Floor type. Glides assume a hard floor; for carpet use rigid plastic skids instead.

item.title: Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Woods Studios / Vermont Furniture Designs Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console Table (product page, archive), with the proportions held to the maker’s published numbers. A long, low console: a wide, thin top that overhangs the leg frame by a lot at the ends, two shallow drawers hung right under the top, and a narrow lower shelf carried on chunky side rails.

Provenance of the numbers. Dimensions marked (stated) come straight from the maker’s Dimensions and Construction Details panels. Dimensions marked (derived) are worked out from the stated ones so everything closes. Dimensions marked (est.) are measured off the maker’s front and three-quarter photos — good to roughly ±¼″ — and are the ones to sanity-check against the real piece, or against your own taste, before cutting.

Stated by the maker

Item Value
Overall 60″ W × 16″ D × 29″ H (stated)
Top overhang, ends 8″ (stated)
Top overhang, front/back 1″ (stated)
Drawer front (exterior) 19.75″ W × 3.5″ H (stated)
Drawer interior 18″ W × 7.5″ D × 2″ H (stated)
Bottom shelf 41.5″ W × 9.75″ D (stated)
Species Cherry, maple or walnut (stated)
Drawers Dovetailed; beech sides, back and bottom; metal slides; walnut pulls (stated)
Finish Cherry/walnut: hand-rubbed linseed oil + wax. Maple: tung oil + wax (stated)

Drawings (true scale)

All three are drawn at 1″ = 12 px from the dimensions on this page, so they can be measured against each other. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

The ratios

Everything hangs off the 60″ overall width and the 8″ / 1″ overhangs. The frame is whatever is left:

Derived Working Result
Leg frame, width 60 − 2 × 8 44″ (derived)
Leg frame, depth 16 − 2 × 1 14″ (derived)
Frame opening between front legs 44 − 2 × 1¾ 40½″ (derived)
Two drawer fronts + divider + reveals 2 × 19.75 + ¾ + 4 × 1/16 40½″ (derived — fills the opening exactly)
Shelf width 44 − 2 × 1¼ (side-rail thickness) 41½″ (derived — matches stated shelf width)
Shoulder-to-shoulder, front↔back 14 − 2 × 1¾ 10½″ (derived; shelf is 9¾″, leaving ¾″)

That the two independent checks (drawers fill 40½″; shelf lands on 41½″ with 1¼″ rails) both close is the evidence that the 1¾″ legs and 1¼″-thick side rails are right.

Proportion Value
Width : height 60 : 29 ≈ 2.07 : 1
Width : depth 60 : 16 = 3.75 : 1
Frame width ÷ overall width 44 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.733 (each end overhang = 13.3 %)
Drawer front width ÷ overall width 19.75 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.33
Drawer front height ÷ overall height 3.5 ÷ 29 ≈ 0.12
Leg width ÷ overall height 1¾ ÷ 29 ≈ 0.06
Shelf top height ÷ overall height ≈ 10½ ÷ 29 ≈ 0.36 (est.)

To resize: multiply every dimension by one factor k (so 48″ long → k = 0.8) and the proportions hold. Round leg and rail sections to stock, but do not change the 8″-end / 1″-front overhang ratio independently of the width — the long ends are the look.

Dimensions that are estimates

Item Value Basis
Top thickness ¾″ (est.) ≈ 14 px against a 3.5″ drawer front at ≈ 66 px in the front photo. Could be 1″; ¾″ keeps the 8″ cantilever light
Leg section 1¾″ square (est.) ≈ 1.85″ measured, and 1¾″ is what makes both closures above work
Shelf top above floor ≈ 10½″ (est.) Front photo, scaled against the 29″ height
Lower drawer rail ¾″ thick × 1″ tall (est.) Thin strip under the drawers in the front photo
Center divider ¾″ wide (est.) Narrow stile between the drawers
Side aprons 4½″ tall (est.) Solid panel under the top at the ends in the three-quarter photo
Pull 8″ × ⅝″ × 1″ (est.), walnut ≈ 8″ long against the 19.75″ drawer front; stand-off finger pull

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length — 1″ tenons are baked into rail and apron lengths. Species: cherry (or maple/walnut) for the case; beech (or maple) for drawer boxes.

Case

Part Qty T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 1¾″ × 1¾″ × 28¼″ 8/4 stock. Height = 29 − ¾ top
Lower front rail 1 ¾″ × 1″ × 42½″ Under the drawers; 40½″ between shoulders; 1″ tenons
Back apron 1 ¾″ × 4½″ × 42½″ 1″ tenons
Side aprons 2 ¾″ × 4½″ × 12½″ 10½″ between shoulders; 1″ tenons
Center divider 1 ¾″ × ¾″ × 3⅝″ Underside of top to lower front rail; pinned to the front of the center runner
Center runner 1 ¾″ × 3″ × 12½″ Lower front rail to back apron, centered; slides mount on both faces. Housed in both
Slide spacers 2 1″ × 3″ × 9″ Screwed to the inside of the side aprons so the slide face sits at the drawer-box edge
Shelf side rails 2 1¼″ × 2½″ × 12½″ Flush to leg outer faces; 10½″ between shoulders; top ≈ 11″ off floor
Shelf cleats 2 ¾″ × ¾″ × 9¾″ Glue/screw to rail inner faces to carry the shelf
Shelf 1 ¾″ × 9¾″ × 41½″ Sits between the side rails, centered front-to-back (⅜″ setback each side)
Top 1 ¾″ × 16″ × 60″ Floats; buttons or figure-8s, never glued

The runner and spacers are sized for ½″-per-side slides — adjust them if the slides you buy need more or less clearance.

Drawers (×2, identical)

Part Qty each T × W × L Notes
Front 1 ¾″ × 3½″ × 19¾″ Cherry, grain-matched to the case; 1/16″ reveals all round
Sides 2 ½″ × 2½″ × 8½″ Beech; dovetailed to front and back
Back 1 ½″ × 2½″ × 18″ (between sides) Beech
Bottom 1 ¼″ × as fitted Beech; in a groove, floating
Pull 1 8″ × ⅝″ × 1″ Walnut; two screws from the inside

The stated 18″ × 7½″ × 2″ interior sets the drawer box: 18″ clear between sides gives a box about 19″ wide overall, so ½″-per-side slides fit the 19.875″ opening. The 7½″ box depth sits in a 14″ frame, so there is room behind the drawers — decide whether to close it with a back panel (the maker uses plywood backs on case pieces) or leave it open.

Build sequence

  1. Mill legs from 8/4 and everything else to size; let stock sit between passes — cherry moves.
  2. Cut mortises and tenons (5/16″–⅜″ mortises, 1″ deep). Miter tenon tips where two meet inside a leg.
  3. Dry-fit the two end frames: leg pair + side apron + shelf side rail. Confirm the 10½″ shoulder distance and that the rail sits flush to the leg outer face.
  4. Glue up the ends, then join them with the front and back aprons and the lower front rail. Dry-clamp first and check the 40½″ opening and the 44″ × 14″ frame for square. Drawbore if you like — optional here, since the top and drawers add little racking load.
  5. Fit the center runner and divider and check the two drawer openings are equal (≈ 19⅞″ each with 1/16″ reveals).
  6. Screw on the slide spacers, add the shelf cleats and drop in the shelf. The shelf carries load, so keep the cleats glued and screwed.
  7. Build and dovetail the drawers, fit the slides, then trim the fronts to a 1/16″ reveal.
  8. Make the walnut pulls and fit them.
  9. Finish: hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax for cherry and walnut (tung oil and wax for maple), matching the maker. Scrape off all squeeze-out first.
  10. Attach the top with buttons so it can move seasonally. Center it: 8″ at each end, 1″ front and back.

Domino option

A Festool Domino can cut most of the joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The 5/16″ mortise in this plan matches an 8 mm Domino; a 40 mm Domino goes 20 mm (¾″) into each part, a 50 mm Domino 25 mm (1″).

Rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside the leg, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them. (The hand-cut plan avoids this by mitering tenon tips, which a loose tenon can’t do.)

Joint Domino Cut length (was)
Back apron (¾″ × 4½″) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 25 mm below the apron’s top edge 40½″ (42½″)
Side aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 70 mm below the apron’s top edge 10½″ (12½″)
Lower front rail (¾″ × 1″) 1 × 4×20 per end, centred on the rail 40½″ (42½″)
Shelf side rails (×2, 1¼″ × 2½″) 1 × 8×50 per end, centred 10½″ (12½″)
Center runner Keep it housed in the lower front rail and back apron 12½″ (unchanged)
  • With the Domino, cut length = shoulder-to-shoulder (40½″ and 10½″).
  • At the back legs the back apron (upper) and side apron (lower) are staggered. At the front legs the side apron (lower-middle of its 4½″) stays clear of the lower front rail’s 4×20.
  • The 1″ lower front rail is the weak spot — a 4×20 is the largest Domino that fits. It is lightly loaded and the center runner and divider support it, but if you want more, use a shop-made stub tenon.
  • Keep the aprons flush to the leg outer faces and centre each mortise on the part’s thickness.

Open questions

  • Top thickness — ¾″ is estimated; if the real piece reads chunkier, 1″ is the likely answer. Re-check drawer front height (3.5″) against it.
  • Shelf height — about 10½″ to the shelf top is estimated from photos.
  • Frame joinery — the maker’s page does not say how the legs and rails are joined, so mortise-and-tenon here is my choice, to match the other console plan on this site.
  • Space behind the drawers — see the note above.

item.title: Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Furniture Designs Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (product page, archive), with the proportions taken from the maker’s photos and drawing. Three equal drawers stacked under a top that flares out past the case at the ends, four straight legs, an arched apron across the front, and frame-and-panel sides.

Provenance of the numbers. The maker publishes only the overall size and the construction notes. (stated) = from the maker’s page. (derived) = worked out from other numbers here so everything closes. (est.) = measured off the maker’s front photo, dimensioned drawing and three-quarter photo — good to about ±¼″ at best. The front/back overhang in particular is borrowed from a sibling model (the Heartwood Shaker End Table), because it cannot be read from a front view. Check the (est.) items before cutting.

Stated by the maker

Item Value
Overall 24″ W × 18″ D × 28″ H (stated)
Drawers 3, dovetailed; beech sides, backs and bottoms; high-end metal slides (stated)
Knobs Matching hardwood (stated)
Case Solid-wood sides; hardwood-plywood back (stated)
Species Cherry, maple or walnut (stated)
Finish Cherry/walnut: hand-rubbed linseed oil + wax. Maple: tung oil + wax (stated)

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 16 px from the dimensions on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Side elevation

Plan view, top removed

Arched front apron

The ratios

Derived Working Result
Case width 24 − 2 × 2½ (end overhang) 19″ (derived)
Case depth 18 − 2 × 1¼ (front/back overhang) 15½″ (derived)
Drawer opening between legs 19 − 2 × 1½ 16″ (derived — matches the ≈16″ measured on the photo and drawing)
Drawer front width 16 − 2 × 1/16 15⅞″ (derived)
Drawer stack 3 × 6″ + 2 × ¾″ rails + 6 × 1/16″ reveals 19⅞″ (derived)
Floor to bottom of lowest opening 28 − 1 (top) − 19⅞ 7⅛″ (derived — matches ≈ 7¼″ measured)
Front apron, ends / centre 7⅛″ band: ends 2⅝″, centre 1⅝″ 1″ rise (est.)
Proportion Value
Width : height 24 : 28 ≈ 0.86 : 1
Width : depth 24 : 18 = 4 : 3
Case width ÷ overall width 19 ÷ 24 ≈ 0.79 (each end overhang ≈ 10.4 %)
Drawer front height ÷ width 6 ÷ 15⅞ ≈ 0.38
Drawer stack ÷ overall height 19⅞ ÷ 28 ≈ 0.71
Floor to opening ÷ overall height 7⅛ ÷ 28 ≈ 0.25

To resize: multiply every dimension by one factor k and the proportions hold; round the stock thicknesses (¾″ rails, 1½″ legs) to what you have and keep the drawer fronts equal.

Dimensions that are estimates

Item Value Basis
End overhang 2½″ ≈ 2½″ scaled off both the front photo and the dimensioned drawing
Front/back overhang 1¼″ Not visible from the front; matches the maker’s Heartwood Shaker End Table (listed 1¼″ front/back, 2″ sides)
Top thickness 1″ (thin edge, bevelled underneath) ≈ 1″ in the front photo; the three-quarter photo shows the edge tapered to roughly ⅜″
Leg section 1½″ square ≈ 1.5″ in the drawing; ≈ 1.1–1.4″ in the photos, so it may be a little lighter. 1½″ makes the 16″ opening close
Drawer front height 6″ ≈ 6.0″ in both straight-on views
Rails between drawers ¾″ ≈ 0.85″ visible including reveals
Knob 1¼″ diameter, centred on each front Round, ≈ 1¼″ in the front photo
Top side rail / muntin 1½″ / 1″ Three-quarter photo shows a top rail, one centre muntin and two panels per side
Slide clearance ½″ per side Typical side-mount metal slide; confirm against the slide you buy

Cut list

T × W × L, cut to length. 1″ tenons are baked into rail lengths. Cherry for the case and drawer fronts; beech (or maple) for drawer boxes.

Case

Part Qty Stock T × W × L Notes
Legs 4 8/4 1½″ × 1½″ × 27″ Height 28 − 1 top. Soft radius on the foot end, as in the photo
Front apron (arched) 1 4/4 ¾″ × 2⅝″ × 18″ Arch cut on the bottom edge: 1″ rise over the 16″ between shoulders (radius 32½″) — see the apron drawing
Front rails 2 4/4 ¾″ × ¾″ × 18″ Between drawers. 16″ between shoulders
Back top rail 1 4/4 ¾″ × 1½″ × 18″ Grooved for the back panel
Back bottom rail 1 4/4 ¾″ × 2⅝″ × 18″ Straight; grooved for the back panel
Back panel 1 ¼″ hardwood ply ¼″ × 16⅜″ × 19⅜″ Floats in grooves (stated: plywood back)
Top side rails 2 4/4 ¾″ × 1½″ × 14½″ 12½″ between shoulders; flush to leg outer face
Bottom side rails (arched) 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2⅝″ × 14½″ Same 1″-rise arch as the front, here over 12½″
Side muntins 2 4/4 ¾″ × 1″ × as fitted Between top and bottom side rails; grooved both edges
Side panels 4 4/4 resawn ½″ × 6⅜″ × 19⅛″ Two per side; float in ⅜″ grooves (width and height include groove depth, less ⅛″)
Slide spacers 2 4/4 ¾″ × 2″ × 12″ Screwed to the inside of the side frames so the slide face sits at the drawer-box edge
Top 1 4/4 1″ × 18″ × 24″ Floats on buttons; underside bevelled toward the edge

(Rails and aprons are shown flush to the leg faces on the outside. Side-rail tenons are about 5/16″ thick; the front-rail tenon is short because the rail is only ¾″ tall — use ¼″ × ½″.)

Drawers (× 3, identical)

Part Qty each T × W × L Notes
Front 1 ¾″ × 6″ × 15⅞″ Cherry, grain-matched top to bottom; 1/16″ reveals
Sides 2 ½″ × 5″ × 12″ Beech; dovetailed
Back 1 ½″ × 4½″ × 14″ Beech; dovetailed
Bottom 1 ¼″ × as fitted Beech; floats in a groove
Knob 1 1¼″ ⌀ Matching cherry, turned or shaped

The box is 15″ wide overall (½″ slide clearance each side of the 16″ opening), so its interior is about 14″ wide — close to the 14¼″ the maker lists for a sibling nightstand. Box length of 12″ fits a 12″ slide with room behind for the back panel.

Build sequence

  1. Mill the 8/4 for legs, then the 4/4 in stages, resting between passes.
  2. Cut mortises and tenons for the legs. Cut the two arches on the front apron and the bottom side rails before assembly.
  3. Groove the side rails, muntins and legs for the panels. Make the four panels, finish them before assembly so no bare wood shows when they move.
  4. Glue up each side frame (legs + top rail + bottom rail + muntin + two panels). Drawbore the leg joints if you like.
  5. Join the two sides with the front apron, the two front rails and the back rails. Dry-clamp first; the opening must be 16″ and the case 19″ × 15½″.
  6. Slide the back panel into its grooves before the last rail goes in.
  7. Screw on the slide spacers, then build and dovetail the three drawers and hang them on the slides.
  8. Make and fit the knobs.
  9. Finish with hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax (cherry), matching the maker.
  10. Attach the top with buttons so it can move seasonally. Centre it: 2½″ at each end, 1¼″ front and back.

Domino option

A Domino is a poor fit for the leg joints on this piece, and a good fit for the muntins.

Why: the 1½″ legs take several joints at the same height. At each back corner, the back top rail and the top side rail both enter at the top; at every corner the arched aprons and bottom rails (2⅝″ tall) meet at the same level. Two Domino mortises from adjacent faces cross inside the leg, so they would have to be staggered in height, and 1½″ and 2⅝″ parts don’t have room to stagger. The hand-cut plan avoids the collision by mitering tenon tips.

Joint Option Notes
Leg joints (rails, aprons) Hand-cut or router-cut tenons, tips mitered As in the cherry console plan
Front rails (¾″ × ¾″) Stub tenon A ¾″-tall rail is too small for a standard Domino (a 4×20 does not fit)
Side muntins (¾″ × 1″, ×2) 1 × 4×20 Domino per end Fits the 1″ width; cut the muntin shoulder-to-shoulder
Back panel, side panels Unchanged Float in grooves
  • If you still want Dominoes at the leg corners, stagger by height and widen the legs to 1¾″ so the mortises have room — but that changes the 16″ opening, so every other dimension on the page moves with it.

Open questions

  • Front/back overhang — 1¼″ is borrowed from the sibling model; the three-quarter photo suggests it is in that range but doesn’t prove it.
  • Leg section — 1½″ closes the 16″ opening, but the photos read as slightly lighter. If you go to 1¼″, either widen the case to 19½″ or widen the opening to 16½″ and the drawer fronts to 16⅜″.
  • Drawer depth — 12″ box length is my choice; the maker doesn’t state it.

item.title: Jeweler's Traveling Tool Chest (Proposed)
item.description:
A tool chest for a jeweler who solders rings and pendants and teaches lapidary workshops (domed cabochons and flat/faceted stones). It has to do two jobs: sit on a bench as a daily soldering kit, and travel to a workshop with a lapidary teaching kit. Two classic chest styles fit; this page compares them, then lays out a proposed build modeled on Mike Pekovich’s traveling tool chest, resized and re-organized for jewelry and lapidary tools.

Provenance of the numbers. Pekovich’s chest is a course product, and its page publishes no dimensions, species or drawer count, so this is a design inspired by it, not a copy. (stated) = from the course page. (derived) = worked out from the sizes I chose so everything closes. (est.) = typical sizes of tools and supplies, which vary by brand: put your own tools on the bench and check them before cutting.

The finished chest (concept rendering)

Nothing here is built yet, so this is a drawing from the plan sizes, not a photograph.

Two styles to choose from

Pekovich traveling chest Dutch tool chest
Shape Rectangular case, flat frame-and-panel lid, drawers under an open well Sloped lid, two tiers, fall front (see below)
Made to Be carried: side handles, lock, modest size Hold a full set of woodworking hand tools
Strength Tidy small tools: lift-out tray, two drawers, lockable Big tools: planes, saws, chisels, in a light pine box
Weak point here A well too shallow for long tools Jeweler’s tools are small and need separating; a big open well does not give you that

Pick: the Pekovich style. A jeweler’s kit is hundreds of small, fragile or expensive pieces (stones, laps, burs, solder). They want dividers, a lock, and a carry size, and not a big open well. The standard Dutch chest, described next, is the better answer for planes and saws.

The standard Dutch tool chest

For comparison, this is the chest the Dutch style is known for: a woodworker’s tool chest, not a jeweler’s. I read two pages for it, so what follows is what they say and little more. Christopher Schwarz’s book Dutch Tool Chests is the place for dimensions and joinery; I could not open that page.

Item What the sources say
Lid “Perhaps the chest’s most distinctive characteristic is its sloped lid” (stated, Fine Woodworking). A search summary of a Schwarz video gives about 30°; I did not confirm it
Tiers A top tier for chisels, saws, planes and layout tools, and a bottom sized for molding and joinery planes and tool rolls (stated, Fine Woodworking)
Fall front Has battens; they work best when set no more than ⅛″ inside the case sides (stated, Fine Woodworking)
Joinery Dovetails at the bottom only, plus dadoes, rabbets and cut nails (stated, Fine Woodworking); screws are not required, and cut nails or wooden pegs work (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Wood Pine “or another lightweight wood”; “the cheapest, lightest wood that is available” (stated)
Size One build’s interior depth is 11¼″, the width of a 1×12 (stated, Fine Woodworking). Overall sizes are not stated in what I could read; the “big” chest is said to hold as many tools as a full-size English floor chest (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Hardware and finish Strap hinges and lifts; commonly painted, historically often blue (stated, Popular Woodworking)
Not found Overall dimensions, the side profile, dado heights, and any sliding or saw till

What it means for a jeweler’s chest. The Dutch chest suits a woodworker’s long, heavy tools in a light box that is simple to build. A jeweler’s kit is small and needs separating, which is why this page builds the Pekovich style. The one idea worth borrowing is the two tiers: small tools on top, heavier ones below. The proposed chest already does this with its tray and drawers.

What Pekovich’s course covers (stated)

From the course page (archive), titled Build a Traveling Tool Chest with Mike Pekovich:

Item Value
Corner joints Dovetails at the bottom corners, tails cut at the table saw (stated)
Shelf Through-tenons, laid out together with the mortises (stated)
Case assembly Glued up, tenons wedged, then drilled and pinned (stated)
Case front Mortised for a lid lock (stated)
Lid Frame-and-panel, with bridle joints at the corners (stated)
Drawers Pinned rabbet drawers (stated)
Storage Lift-out mitered trays, slotted blocks for saws, other tool-holding features (stated)
Level / length Intermediate; over 10 hours of instruction; downloadable plans (stated)
Not stated Overall size, species, drawer count, hinge type, handles

If you build from this page, buy the course for the joinery: this page does not teach it.

What the chest has to do

  • Hold two kits that are never used at the same time. Soldering (daily, bench) and lapidary (workshop days) go in separate drawers, so you can lift out one kit.
  • Stay light enough to carry. The case alone is about 22 lb in cherry (derived: ½″ case parts, ¾″ shelf and bottom, cherry at about 35 lb/ft³). Tools add roughly 15–20 lb (est.). Plan on two bail handles and, at about 40 lb loaded, a second person for stairs.
  • Keep the abrasives apart. In cabbing, a single grain of a coarse grit on a fine pad leaves scratches that cost a whole polishing step. Each grit gets its own sealed jar, and laps stay in their own sleeves.
  • Keep acid and water out. Pickle (Sparex or citric) and wet lapidary slurry corrode steel tools and stain wood. The chest holds dry, clean tools only; carry wet items in a separate tub.
  • Protect metal and stones. Many woods give off organic acids, and oak is the usual one to avoid near steel and silver. Use cherry or maple, finish the inside with dewaxed shellac, and wax it. Keep loose stones in lidded boxes or gem papers, not in open tray compartments.
  • Be lockable. A half-mortise lid lock (the course installs one) deters casual theft but does not stop a determined one. A chest with stones and precious metal also needs insurance, which a lock does not replace.

The proposed chest

Overall 22″ W × 12″ D × 13¾″ H (derived: chosen so a 21″ interior fits files and a 12″ mandrel with room), with a lift-out tray and a drawer bay of two equal drawers.

Item Value
Overall 22″ × 12″ × 13¾″ (derived)
Case height / lid 13″ case + ¾″ lid (derived)
Case parts ½″ sides, back and well front; ¾″ bottom and shelf (derived)
Well front 4½″ tall (derived)
Drawer bay 7″: two openings 3¼″ with a ½″ rail between (derived)
Drawer fronts 20⅞″ × 3³⁄₁₆″, ¹⁄₁₆″ reveals (derived)
Drawer interior about 20⅛″ × 9⅝″ × 2¾″ (derived)
Tray 20¾″ × 10¾″ × 1¾″, resting on ½″ cleats (derived)
Species Cherry or maple case, maple drawer sides (proposed)

Drawings (true scale)

Drawn at 1″ = 24 px from the sizes on this page. Click to open full size.

Front elevation

Cross-section at centre

Lift-out tray

Drawer layouts

What goes where

Zone Contents Why here
Tray Pliers and cutters (jaws up in a slotted block), needle and hand files, dividers, calipers, steel rule, ring sizer, burnishers, pushers, scribes, burs in index cases, loupes Used constantly on both kinds of day; lift the tray out and the well is clear
Well (about 2¼″ under the tray) Hammers and mallets, a 12″ ring mandrel (bracelet mandrel if it fits), saw frame and blades, torch tips Heavier, longer, or used less often
Top drawer: soldering Solder sheet and wire in labeled tubes, flux, borax dish, tweezers, third hand, a ceramic tile, ring clamp, spare bench-pin inserts, lidded boxes for work in progress Daily bench kit; sits right under the tray
Bottom drawer: lapidary Dop sticks on edge in a slotted rack, dop wax, one sealed jar per grit and polish, cabochon templates, calipers, loupes, gem tweezers, wrapped stones, faceting laps in padded sleeves Heavy, so it rides low; opens fully for a workshop table
Not in the chest Torch, hoses and fuel; pickle pot; wet grinders, saws and the faceting machine; anything wet Fire, acid and water; the workshop venue normally supplies the machines (see Open questions)

Fire. The chest is a wooden box. Close it before lighting a torch, keep it out of the soldering area, and never leave a hot tile, torch or alcohol lamp on or inside it.

Cut list (proposed)

Finished sizes in inches, thickness × width × length. Check against your own layout before cutting.

Part Qty Size Notes
Sides 2 ½ × 12 × 13 Dovetailed to the well front and back; grooved for the bottom and shelf
Well front 1 ½ × 4½ × 21 Mortised for the lid lock
Back 1 ½ × 21 × 12¼ Rabbeted into the sides
Bottom 1 ¾ × 11½ × 21 In grooves in the sides
Shelf 1 ¾ × 11½ × 22 Through-tenoned into the sides: 22″ includes the tenons
Drawer rail 1 ½ × ¾ × 21 Full depth
Lid frame 4 ¾ × 2 × 22 (long), ¾ × 2 × 12 (short) Bridle corners, grooved ¼″ for the panel
Lid panel 1 ¼ × 8⅜ × 18⅜ Floats in the groove
Drawer fronts 2 ¾ × 3³⁄₁₆ × 20⅞ Pulls: small wire rings
Drawer sides 4 ⅜ × 3 × 10 Maple
Drawer backs 2 ⅜ × 2¾ × 20⅛
Drawer bottoms 2 ¼ × 9⅝ × 20⅛
Tray cleats 2 ½ × ½ × 21 Top face 10¾″ above the floor
Tray 1 set ⅜ sides, ¼ bottom, ¼ dividers Mitered

Hardware: two butt hinges and a cord or chain stay (as in the photo), one half-mortise lock, two bail handles, two ring pulls.

Build order

  1. Mock up and check the tools. Lay your actual tools on the tray and drawer footprints. Move dividers before cutting any wood. Most fixes here cost nothing.
  2. Mill the stock and cut the sides, well front, back, bottom and shelf to length.
  3. Cut the joints: dovetails for the well front and back, grooves for the bottom, rabbet for the back, mortises for the shelf’s through-tenons.
  4. Dry-fit, then glue the case. Wedge and pin the shelf tenons.
  5. Make the lid: bridle-jointed frame, floating panel, then hang it with two butt hinges and fit the stay and the lock.
  6. Fit the drawer rail, make the drawers, then plane the fronts to ¹⁄₁₆″ reveals.
  7. Make the tray and cleats, and cut the dividers last so they fit the finished drawers.
  8. Finish: dewaxed shellac inside, shellac and wax outside. Let it cure fully before you load the tools.
  9. Handles and pulls.

Open questions

  • What the workshops supply. This plan assumes the venue provides the grinders, trim saw and faceting machine, so the chest carries only hand tools and consumables. If you bring a faceting head or a small cab machine, it needs its own case.
  • The meaning of “flat/faceted ground.” I read it as flat-lapped and faceted stones next to domed cabochons. If it means something else, the laps and dops section changes.
  • Lap size. The laps drawer assumes 6″ discs. 8″ laps do not fit a 9⅝″ drawer with their sleeves, so check yours.
  • Weight. About 22 lb empty is heavy for a chest that will go up stairs. Basswood or poplar drawers, or ⅜″ case parts, save about 4 lb; I kept ½″ for the dovetails and handles.
  • Hinge, lock and handle choices. The course page does not name them; the ones above are my choice.
